subject: Computer Networking
title: What Happens When You Hit Enter
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on What Happens When You Hit Enter.

hook.text: You type 'google.com' and press Enter. In under a second, a page appears. What just happened?

buildup.text: Your browser asks a DNS server to translate 'google.com' into an IP address — the server's real location.

discovery.text: Then your browser opens a TCP connection and sends an HTTP request asking for the page's content.

twist.text: The response might come from a server thousands of miles away — or from a CDN cache across town.

climax.text: Your browser receives HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images, then assembles the page you see on screen.

punchline.text: One keystroke. DNS, TCP, HTTP, render. Done.

quiz.question: What is the first step after you type a URL and hit Enter?
options: DNS resolves the domain name to an IP address
The server sends a push notification

details.summary: Typing a URL and pressing Enter triggers a cascade: DNS resolves the domain to an IP, TCP establishes a connection via three-way handshake, TLS negotiates encryption, HTTP sends the request, and the server responds with HTML that the browser renders into a visible page.
details.whyItMatters: This single action involves dozens of protocols and systems working in milliseconds. Understanding the chain explains slow loads, errors, and security.
takeaways: DNS resolution converts the domain name to an IP address
TCP and TLS establish a secure connection before data flows
The browser parses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to render the page

faq.question: How long does this entire process typically take?
faq.answer: A simple page load takes 100 to 500 milliseconds. DNS lookup takes 10 to 100ms, TCP handshake adds one round trip, TLS adds another. The server response and rendering take the rest. CDNs and caching reduce these times by serving content from nearby locations.

faq.question: What is the most common cause of slow page loads?
faq.answer: Server response time and large page resources are the most common causes. Too many JavaScript files, unoptimized images, and render-blocking resources slow page display. DNS lookup delays and distant servers add latency. Browser caching eliminates much of this on repeat visits.
